The Sons of the Stranger
thuh SUNZ uv thuh STRAYN-jur
n. phr. (the foreigners joined to the LORD, Isaiah 56:6)
Hebrew b'nē hannēkār — sons of the foreignness; nēkār denotes what is foreign or alien, distinct from gēr, the resident sojourner already provided for in the Law.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 56 opens the house of God wider than the returning exiles expected. The eunuch who keeps the sabbath is promised a name better than of sons and of daughters, and then: Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD, to serve him, and to love the name of the LORD, to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant; and then the promise — Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer. The chapter ends with the sentence our Lord quoted when He cleansed the temple: mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people. Two guards keep the passage from being what it is often made. The welcome is not unconditional — it is given to those who join themselves to the LORD, love His name, keep His sabbath and take hold of His covenant, which is to say to converts, not to foreigners as such. And it is not a late innovation; Solomon had prayed at the dedication that the LORD would hear the stranger who came out of a far country for His name's sake. The passage is the Old Testament's plainest anticipation of the Gentile ingathering, and Paul's language of those who were afar off being made nigh by the blood of Christ is its fulfilment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Stranger, a foreigner; one who belongs to another country. Join, to unite; to associate. Isaiah 56:6, the foreigner who takes hold of the covenant.

expand to see more

Stranger, a foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not a native.

Stranger, one unknown; a guest; one not admitted to communication or fellowship.

Join, to unite; to couple; to associate; to confederate.

Hebrew nēkār, that which is foreign or alien; distinct from gēr, a sojourner.

House of prayer for all people, Isaiah 56:7, quoted by Christ in Mark 11:17.

Key Scripture

Isa 56:3 — "Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people: neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree."

Isa 56:6 — "Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD, to serve him, and to love the name of the LORD, to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant;"

Isa 56:7 — "Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people."

Eph 2:13 — "But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ."

Modern Corruption

The passage is made a charter for admitting all comers on their own terms, with the covenant conditions Isaiah states quietly dropped; or it is confined to ethnic Israel's future and denied to the church.

expand to see more

The modern use of Isaiah 56 is as a text of unconditional welcome: God's house is open to everyone, full stop, and any requirement laid on the newcomer is read as the exclusion the chapter condemns. Isaiah says something more generous and more demanding. The sons of the stranger are brought to the holy mountain, and they are described in the same sentence as joining themselves to the LORD, serving Him, loving His name, keeping His sabbath and taking hold of His covenant. The welcome is real and it is to a covenant, not around one. What the chapter forbids is the man who has done all this being told he is still an outsider by blood; what it does not do is dispense with the joining.

The opposite error assigns the promise wholly to a future national Israel and withholds it from the church, which empties the chapter of the use the New Testament actually makes of it. Our Lord quoted verse seven against the traders in the court of the Gentiles — the very place where the sons of the stranger were to pray — and Paul tells the Ephesians that they who were sometime far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ, and are no more strangers and foreigners but fellowcitizens with the saints. The principle to recover is that the Gentile ingathering was promised in the prophets before it was accomplished in Acts, and that it was always a covenant ingathering.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew b'nē hannēkār, sons of the foreigner — brought to the holy mountain on the terms of joining, loving, keeping and taking hold.

expand to see more

Hebrew nēkār, foreignness or alien descent; b'nē hannēkār, its sons.

Distinguished from gēr, the resident sojourner of the Mosaic law.

Hebrew lāvāh, to join oneself, cleave to, be attached.

Hebrew chāzaq bab'rīth, to take hold of the covenant, Isaiah 56:6.

Solomon had prayed for the stranger from a far country, 1 Kings 8:41-43.

Usage

"the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD"

"every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant"

"mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people"
